Background . Dengue virus (DENV) infection is the most common arboviral disease that affects tropical and subtropical regions. Based on the clinical hallmarks, the different severities of patients range from mild dengue fever (MDF) to severe dengue diseases (SDDs) and include dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. These are commonly associated with cytokine release syndrome (CRS). Principal Finding . In this study, we created an integrated and precise multiplex panel of cytokine/chemokine assays based on our literature analysis to monitor dengue CRS. A 24-plex panel of cytokines/chemokines was evaluated to measure the plasma levels of targeting factors in dengue patients with an MDF and SDD diagnosis without or with comorbidities. As identified in sixteen kinds of cytokines/chemokines, ten were significantly ( P < 0.05) (10/16) increased, one was significantly ( P < 0.01) (1/16) decreased, and five were potentially (5/16) altered in all dengue patients ( n = 30) in the acute phase of disease onset. Compared to MDF, the levels of IL-8 (CXCL-8) and IL-18 in SDD were markedly ( P < 0.05) increased, accompanied by positively increased IL-6 and TNF- α and decreased IFN- γ and RANTES. With comorbidities, SDD significantly ( P < 0.01) portrayed elevated IL-18 accompanied by increased IL-6 and decreased IFN- α 2 and IL-12. In addition, decreased platelets were significantly ( P < 0.05) associated with increased IL-18. Significance . These results demonstrate an efficient panel of dengue cytokine/chemokine assays used to explore the possible level of CRS during the acute phase of disease onset; also, we are the first to report the increase of IL-18 in severe dengue with comorbidity compared to severe dengue without comorbidity and mild dengue. Introduction Dengue virus (DENV) is the most prevalent arboviral disease in tropical and subtropical regions [ 1 ], which provides the ideal breeding ground for its primary vector, the Aedes mosquitoes. It is estimated that 100–400 million people in the world population are infected by DENV infection yearly [ 2 ]. DENV infection can be broadly classified according to the degree of severity into mild dengue fever (MDF) and severe dengue diseases (SDDs). The latter can be further distinguished into dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) and dengue shock syndrome (DSS), which encompass various symptoms such as circulatory failure or shock, multiorgan failure, and central nervous system (CNS) impairment, which needs intensive treatment and monitoring [ 3 , 4 ]. This condition exposes patients to a higher risk of death since no effective antiviral treatment is available for dengue infection, and the vaccine has inconsistent effectiveness against the four dengue serotypes [ 5 – 7 ]. Various factors influence the clinical course severity, including virus, host, and environmental factors [ 8 ]. The danger of dengue infection also building up in the secondary dengue infection patients as antibodies from the previous infection is being unable to neutralize the virus from heterologous infection, facilitating virus entrance to the Fc-presenting cell, causing higher viral replication and severe infection, known as antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) [ 9 – 13 ]. In addition, high virus titers can promote overactivation of the immune system and excessive secretion of proinflammatory cytokines, known as cytokine storms or cytokine release syndrome (CRS). This condition may contribute to various symptoms seen in dengue severity [ 14 – 16 ]. Some previous studies have shown that some cytokines are increased in response to severe dengue infection, such as TNF- α , MCP-1 (CCL-2), RANTES (CCL-5), IFN- γ , IP-10 (CXCL-10), IL-4, IL-6, IL-8 (CXCL-8), IL-10, and GM-CSF (CSF-2) [ 17 – 20 ]. Therefore, changes in the cytokine level might represent some specific event that determines the disease progression. For instance, viral protein nonstructural 1 (NS1) from DENV-infected cells [ 21 ] as well as an ADE infectious condition [ 22 ] can induce IL-10 production from monocytes. In DENV infection, IL-10 suppresses the DENV-specific T-cell response [ 23 ], supporting viral survival and replication and increasing disease severity. On the other hand, a low IFN- γ level correlates with a high viral load and more severe symptoms [ 24 ], indicating its essential role in early virus elimination and a better disease outcome. Despite all the previous research, no cytokine marker was approved to predict the severity of dengue. Based on previous observations, a twenty-four-cytokine panel was developed and confirmed using a dengue patient's plasma. We checked their level using a multiplex assay, along with the patient's clinical characteristics. The correlations between severity, clinical characteristics, and cytokine levels were analyzed accordingly.

extracted_data.document_summary: This observational study aimed to identify biomarkers for predicting severe dengue disease progression and cytokine release syndrome (CRS) by evaluating an integrated multiplex panel of cytokines/chemokines and clinical parameters in adult dengue patients. Researchers compared various severity groups (mild, severe without/with comorbidities, and healthy controls) across acute and convalescent phases. Key findings highlighted how specific markers like IL-18, IL-8, IL-6, and IFN-γ are altered in severe dengue, particularly with comorbidities, and their correlation with clinical indicators such as platelet counts and NS1. The study also characterized demographic and clinical parameters across patient groups, confirming the utility of a 24-plex cytokine/chemokine panel designed based on extensive literature review.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study on biomarker identification and monitoring for dengue disease progression and severity
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study on 30 adult dengue patients (mean age 61.6 years, 17 male, 13 female) categorized into three severity groups based on WHO criteria (1997 and 2009): Mild Dengue Fever (MDF, n=10), Severe Dengue Disease without comorbidities (SDD-C, n=10), and Severe Dengue Disease with comorbidities (SDD+C, n=10). Six healthy controls were also included. A 24-plex panel of cytokines/chemokines was used to measure plasma levels, along with clinical blood parameters. Blood samples were collected during the acute febrile phase (before 6 days from disease onset) and the convalescent phase (9-18 days from disease onset). No therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were reported, as the study focused on natural disease progression and biomarker correlation with severity.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level; Protein Concentration; Cytokine Level

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased in all dengue cases compared with healthy subjects; significant increase in acute febrile phase (P < 0.05), being one of the top three cytokines with highest significant differences (P ≤ 0.001) in acute dengue vs healthy. Markedly increased (P < 0.05) in Severe Dengue Disease (SDD) compared to Mild Dengue Fever (MDF), significantly higher in SDD (P = 0.037) and showing an increasing trend over twofold in SDD with comorbidities (SDD+C) compared to SDD without comorbidities (SDD-C). Positively linked with IL-6, MIP-1β, IL-15, and MIP-1α, and showed a marked positive relationship with NS1 (r = 0.475, P = 0.011).

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level; Protein Concentration; Cytokine Level; Cytokine/Chemokine Panel (Protein Level)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased in all dengue cases compared with healthy subjects; significant increase in acute febrile phase (P < 0.05), markedly increased (P < 0.05) in SDD compared to MDF, and significantly higher in SDD (P = 0.002). Significantly elevated (P < 0.01) in SDD with comorbidities, showing an increasing trend over twofold in SDD+C compared to SDD-C with the most significant changes found (P < 0.01). Steadily increased significantly across all severity groups and significantly higher in severe dengue compared to healthy samples of patients with mild dengue infection. Positively associated with IL-10, TNF-α, VEGF, and IL-1Rα. Exhibited a significant negative correlation with platelets (r = 0.393, P = 0.031) and NS1 levels in the acute phase of dengue infection, where significant platelet induction caused a considerable increase in serum IL-18.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Proinflammatory cytokine, plays a role in innate and acquired immunity, induces IFN-γ secretion, and is involved in various inflammatory conditions such as sepsis, diabetes, metabolic syndromes, atherosclerosis, and cardiovascular disorders.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Overall acute dengue infection, particularly Severe Dengue Disease (SDD) compared to Mild Dengue Fever (MDF), and especially in SDD with comorbidities. Correlated with platelets, NS1, and other cytokines/chemokines.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A strong and potential biomarker for predicting severe dengue disease progression, particularly when severe and with comorbid groups. It indicates immune overactivation, is associated with platelet activation, and is consistently higher in severe dengue, making it a plausible option for a dengue severity measure. It is involved in dengue Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) and is associated with the development of comorbidities in SDD patients.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased in SDD compared to MDF (decreasing trend, not statistically significant: P = 0.06; x® = 38.4 pg/mL in SDD vs x® = 110.6 pg/mL in MDF). Increased in all dengue cases compared with healthy subjects, but showed an overall reduction in SDD. Higher in the acute febrile phase of dengue patients compared to healthy controls (P < 0.05 for overall acute dengue vs healthy). Levels in the convalescent phase were similar to healthy individuals. analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels indicate more severe symptoms, higher viral load, poorer disease outcome, and impaired early virus elimination. Its initial increase in general dengue cases but subsequent reduction in severe dengue suggests a complex role, with suppression linked to severe dengue outcomes (DHF/DSS) and resembling cytokine involvement in severe dengue progression.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased levels reported. Decreased platelets were significantly (P < 0.05) associated with increased IL-18. measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Highly prevalent, detected in 6 of 7 patients in the MDF group, all (10) patients in the SDD-C group, and 8 of 9 patients in the SDD+C group. Levels were lowest in the MDF group in the acute phase and peaked in the SDD-C group (slightly higher than SDD+C). Levels decreased to near zero in the convalescent phase. Showed a significant negative correlation with platelets (P < 0.01) and IL-18 levels in the acute phase of dengue infection. Exhibited a marked positive relationship with IL-8 (r = 0.475, P = 0.011) and MIP-1α (r = 0.383, P = 0.044).
